headline: High: shared project-directory writes plus broad network egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks; compliance risk is medium due to mixed data classes and third-party API use.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-engineer writes files in a per-project directory with no self-isolation by default, and RD-Agent also uses files/logs plus multiple LLM/API surfaces. That shared workspace makes file-based prompt injection plausible even without a browser bridge. The interaction is documented only indirectly, so I choose medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory or shared log path
IF either agent reads file contents as trusted instructions
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of generated files as prompts
Use read-only mounts for one agent
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and call third-party model APIs by default. gpt-engineer handles OPENAI_API_KEY and RD-Agent handles multiple API keys plus kaggle.json, while both touch filesystem content. If sensitive project data enters either context, it can flow to external inference services; the pairwise leakage path is plausible and not blocked by default.
conditions: IF sensitive source code, logs, or datasets are placed in the shared workspace
IF either agent sends file contents to configured model APIs
mitigations: Rotate and scope API keys narrowly
Block outbound traffic except approved endpoints
requires-engineering: enforce DLP on prompts and attachments

C_capability_conflict.rationale: gpt-engineer can write the project filesystem and spawn subprocesses, while RD-Agent runs in Docker and also uses files/logs and external APIs. Their shared mutable workspace via the project directory creates overlapping write pressure even though RD-Agent's exact write scope is less explicit. Uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same project directory or log tree
IF one agent rewrites files the other is concurrently reading
mitigations: Serialize writes with a lock file

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer writes files and can execute generated code, while RD-Agent is a research/development agent that consumes files and APIs. If RD-Agent treats gpt-engineer's generated artifacts as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream research outputs or actions. The pairwise handoff is plausible but not directly evidenced, so medium fits.
conditions: IF RD-Agent ingests gpt-engineer output without verification
IF generated code or reports are reused as factual inputs
mitigations: requires-engineering: add validation gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: gpt-engineer is documented as handling generated source code, while RD-Agent touches financial reports, competition datasets, execution traces, and logs and uses third-party APIs. That creates a compliance mismatch risk around retention and data-class handling, even though no specific residency or certification conflict is documented. I cite both because the mismatch arises from their combined data scopes.
conditions: IF regulated or sensitive datasets are processed by RD-Agent
IF generated code or logs are retained beyond the operator's policy
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair
requires-engineering: map each data class to an approved processor
